facts.fact: A frog begins life as an egg in the water and hatches as a tadpole, which has a tail, no legs, and breathes with gills like a fish. Over a few weeks it grows back legs, then front legs, and its tail shrinks away before it hops onto land.
facts.hook: the 'little fish' a child keeps in a jar start growing legs

facts.fact: A caterpillar hangs from a twig and hardens into a case called a chrysalis. Inside, its body changes completely, and about two weeks later a butterfly crawls out.
facts.hook: a chrysalis in a jar that everyone thinks has died

facts.fact: A mother sea turtle crawls onto a beach at night, digs a hole with her back flippers, lays about a hundred eggs, covers them with sand and goes back to the sea. The babies hatch about two months later and race to the water by themselves.
facts.hook: a patch of beach marked off with sticks that nobody may step on

facts.fact: A bat is the only mammal that can truly fly. It hunts moths in the dark by making squeaks too high for people to hear and listening for the echoes that bounce back.
facts.hook: a child insists the thing swooping around the barn is a bird

facts.fact: A honeybee that finds flowers flies home and does a wiggle dance on the honeycomb. The direction and length of the dance tell the other bees which way to fly and how far.
facts.hook: a beekeeper's kid tries to read the dance to find the flowers

facts.fact: A snake has no eyelids, so it never blinks; a clear scale covers each eye instead. As it grows it crawls out of its old skin all in one piece, like pulling off a sock.
facts.hook: a whole see-through snake skin found in the woodpile

facts.fact: An owl cannot move its eyes inside its head. Instead it turns its whole head about three quarters of the way around, much farther than a person can, to look behind itself.
facts.hook: a staring contest with the owl in the barn

facts.fact: A camel's hump is a lump of fat, not a bag of water. The camel lives off the fat when there is nothing to eat, and the hump gets smaller and floppy until the camel eats well again.
facts.hook: a child sure the camel at the zoo is carrying a water tank

facts.fact: A penguin is a bird with feathers and a beak, but its wings are stiff flippers that cannot lift it into the air. It uses them to fly underwater, and some penguins can swim faster than a person can run.
facts.hook: a race between a swimmer and a penguin at the aquarium glass

facts.fact: A walking ant leaves a smell trail that other ants follow to food. If you wipe a finger across the trail, the ants coming behind stop at that spot and wander about until they find the smell again.
facts.hook: a line of ants marching to the picnic gets its trail wiped away

facts.fact: An elephant's trunk is its nose and upper lip joined together. It can suck up several liters of water, then squirt the water into its mouth to drink or over its back for a shower.
facts.hook: an elephant gives a surprise shower at the zoo

facts.fact: Whales and dolphins are not fish; they are mammals that breathe air through a blowhole on top of the head. They must come to the surface to breathe, and the spray you see is their warm breath.
facts.hook: spotting a puff of spray far out from a boat

facts.fact: Birds have no teeth. A chicken swallows small stones that sit in a strong muscle bag inside it called a gizzard, and the stones grind its food to bits.
facts.hook: chickens pecking at the gravel path instead of their food

facts.fact: In the cold months a black bear crawls into a den and sleeps for months without eating, drinking, or going to the bathroom. It lives off the fat it put on by eating huge amounts in autumn.
facts.hook: a bear seen eating and eating every day as the leaves fall

facts.fact: A spider is not an insect. Insects have six legs and three body parts, while spiders have eight legs and two body parts and never have wings.
facts.hook: a bug-counting contest where someone counts a spider as an insect

facts.fact: A green plant makes its own food from sunlight, water and air in its leaves. A bean plant grown in a dark cupboard comes up pale yellow and thin and stretches toward any crack of light.
facts.hook: two bean plants, one on the windowsill and one in the closet

facts.fact: Roots always grow down and shoots always grow up. If you plant a seed upside down, the root turns around and heads down anyway.
facts.hook: a child plants a seed upside down on purpose to see what happens

facts.fact: A cloud is made of billions of water drops so tiny that they float in the air. Fog is simply a cloud sitting on the ground, so walking through fog means walking inside a cloud.
facts.hook: a foggy morning walk to school through 'a cloud'

facts.fact: Water in a puddle does not just soak away. On a warm day it slowly turns into vapor, a gas you cannot see, and floats up into the air; draw a chalk line around a puddle and you can watch it shrink in the sun.
facts.hook: a chalk ring around a puddle after the rain

facts.fact: Every snowflake is a tiny ice crystal with six sides or six arms, because of the way water freezes. You can see the shape by catching snowflakes on a dark sleeve and looking closely.
facts.hook: catching snowflakes on a black mitten

facts.fact: Lightning and thunder happen at the same moment, but light reaches you almost instantly while sound takes about three seconds to travel one kilometer. Count the seconds between the flash and the rumble and divide by three to know how many kilometers away the storm is.
facts.hook: counting the seconds as a storm creeps closer to the campsite

facts.fact: A rainbow appears when sunlight shines through water drops with the sun behind you and the rain in front of you. You can make your own with a garden hose on a sunny afternoon by standing with your back to the sun.
facts.hook: trying to make a rainbow with the hose and facing the wrong way

facts.fact: A tree grows a new layer of wood under its bark every year, which shows as a ring on a cut stump. Count the rings from the middle outward and you know how old the tree was.
facts.hook: the old stump in the yard turns out to be older than Grandpa

facts.fact: The yellow and orange colors in an autumn leaf were inside it all summer, hidden by the green. When the days get short, the green breaks down and the other colors show through.
facts.hook: a child wonders where the leaves get their new colors

facts.fact: Plants send their seeds away in different ways. Dandelion seeds ride the wind on fluffy parachutes, burr seeds hook onto animal fur, and berry seeds pass through birds and are dropped far away.
facts.hook: a dog comes home covered in burrs

facts.fact: A pine cone opens its scales in dry air and closes them tight when the air is damp. A pine cone on a windowsill closes up before rain comes.
facts.hook: a pine cone used as a weather forecaster for the picnic

facts.fact: On a sunny day at the seaside the land warms up faster than the water, so warm air over the land rises and cooler air blows in from the sea. That is why a breeze often starts blowing from the water in the afternoon.
facts.hook: a kite that will not fly in the morning but soars after lunch

facts.fact: A young sunflower turns its head to follow the sun across the sky from east to west each day, then swings back to face east during the night. Once it is fully grown, it stops and faces east all the time.
facts.hook: a sunflower that seems to turn its head when nobody is looking

facts.fact: The Earth is tilted, so for half the year the top half leans toward the sun and has summer while the bottom half has winter. In Australia, December is the middle of summer and people can go to the beach at Christmas.
facts.hook: a cousin in Australia sends a photo of Christmas at the beach

facts.fact: A cactus has no leaves; its spines are what its leaves became. It stores water in its thick stem, which is why a cactus can go for months without rain and why a cut cactus is wet inside.
facts.hook: a cactus that got forgotten for the whole summer is still alive

facts.fact: Your heart is a muscle about the size of your fist. In a child it squeezes about 80 times a minute, and you can feel each squeeze as a beat by pressing two fingers on the inside of your wrist.
facts.hook: counting heartbeats before and after a race

facts.fact: A baby is born with about 300 bones, but many of them join together as the child grows. A grown-up has 206 bones.
facts.hook: a child sure that a baby brother has fewer bones than she does

facts.fact: The outside layer of your skin is made of dead cells that flake off all the time while new skin pushes up from underneath. You get a whole new outer layer about every month.
facts.hook: the marker drawing on a hand that fades away in a few days

facts.fact: Your tongue can only taste sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savory. Most of what you call flavor is really smell, which is why food tastes dull when you have a stuffy nose or hold your nose.
facts.hook: a jelly bean guessing game with noses pinched shut

facts.fact: Every hair on your arm has a tiny muscle at its root. When you are cold or scared, these muscles pull the hairs up straight, making the little bumps called goosebumps.
facts.hook: goosebumps appear during a scary story by the campfire

facts.fact: Children have 20 baby teeth. Starting around age six they get loose and fall out one by one, because 32 adult teeth are growing underneath and pushing them out.
facts.hook: a wobbly front tooth on picture day

facts.fact: If you touch something hot, the message from your hand goes to your spinal cord, which sends an order back to pull the hand away before the message even reaches your brain. That is why your hand jumps back before you feel the pain.
facts.hook: a hand that pulls back from the stove before the ouch

facts.fact: Children aged six to twelve need about nine to twelve hours of sleep a night. Your body does most of its growing while you sleep, because the chemical that makes you grow is mostly released at night.
facts.hook: a child who wants to stay up all night to get taller

facts.fact: A broken bone mends itself. New bone grows across the break and joins the pieces, and a cast holds them still so they grow back straight; for a child it takes about six weeks.
facts.hook: a friend's cast that everyone signs

facts.fact: The air you breathe out has less oxygen and more water and carbon dioxide than the air you breathe in. The water in your breath is what fogs up a cold window or a mirror.
facts.hook: writing secret messages in breath-fog on the bus window

facts.fact: Germs are far too small to see; thousands could fit on the tip of a pin. Rubbing your hands with soap for twenty seconds, about the time it takes to sing Happy Birthday twice, lifts them off so the water can rinse them away.
facts.hook: hands that look clean but are not

facts.fact: No two people have the same fingerprints, not even twins. The pattern forms before you are born, stays the same your whole life, and even grows back after a scrape.
facts.hook: a sticky fingerprint on the cookie jar and two suspects

facts.fact: The black dot in the middle of your eye is a hole called the pupil. It gets bigger in the dark to let in more light and shrinks in bright light, and you can watch it change in a mirror with a flashlight.
facts.hook: a flashlight and a mirror in a dark bathroom

facts.fact: Inside each ear is a tiny curved tube full of liquid that tells your brain which way you are moving. When you spin and then stop, the liquid keeps swirling, so your brain thinks you are still turning and you feel dizzy.
facts.hook: spinning in circles until the playground seems to tilt

facts.fact: You have more than 600 muscles, and they can only pull, never push. To bend your arm one muscle pulls, and to straighten it a different muscle on the other side pulls.
facts.hook: feeling the bump on the arm change when lifting a bag

facts.fact: An even number can be split into two equal groups with none left over, and an odd number always has one left over. Add any two odd numbers, like 3 and 5, and the answer is always even, because the two leftovers pair up.
facts.hook: two children with odd bags of marbles pool them and share evenly

facts.fact: Each time you fold a sheet of paper in half, the number of layers doubles: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. After seven folds there are 128 layers, and even a big sheet becomes too thick to fold again.
facts.hook: a bet that nobody can fold a newspaper eight times

facts.fact: There are 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour and 24 hours in a day, so a whole day is 1,440 minutes. Counting one number every second, it takes about 17 minutes to count to 1,000.
facts.hook: a hide-and-seek counter who is told to count to a thousand

facts.fact: On a sunny day your shadow is longest in the early morning and evening and shortest around the middle of the day. People long ago told the time with a stick and its shadow, which is called a sundial.
facts.hook: telling the time on the beach with a stick when no one has a watch

facts.fact: Everyone's foot is a different length, so two people measuring a room in footsteps get different answers. That is why rulers all use the same marks: a centimeter is the same length everywhere.
facts.hook: two friends measure the same room and argue about the answer

facts.fact: You can add numbers in any order and get the same answer: 4 plus 7 is the same as 7 plus 4. Taking away is different: 7 take away 4 is 3, but 4 take away 7 is not 3.
facts.hook: a child checks a sum by adding it backwards

facts.fact: A liter of water weighs one kilogram. A full two-liter bottle weighs two kilograms, and a bathtub of water weighs more than a car.
facts.hook: trying to carry a full water bottle up a hill

facts.fact: Counting one number every second without ever stopping, it would take about 12 days to reach a million. Counting to a hundred takes less than two minutes.
facts.hook: a child who plans to count to a million before dinner

facts.fact: A shape has a line of symmetry if you can fold it so both halves match exactly. A square has four lines of symmetry, a rectangle has only two, and a circle has more than you could ever count.
facts.hook: cutting paper snowflakes from folded squares

facts.fact: A triangle made of three sticks cannot change its shape unless a stick breaks, but a square of four sticks squashes into a diamond. Builders use triangles in bridges and roofs to make them strong.
facts.hook: a straw tower that keeps falling until triangles go in

facts.fact: Some clocks show the hours with letters instead of numbers, called Roman numerals: I is 1, V is 5, X is 10. IV means one less than five, and VI means one more than five.
facts.hook: the old town clock with strange letters instead of numbers

facts.fact: A year is 365 days, but the Earth takes about a quarter of a day longer than that to go around the sun. So every four years February gets an extra day, the 29th, and that year is called a leap year.
facts.hook: a grandmother who has only had a few 'real' birthdays

facts.fact: Cut a pizza into 8 equal slices and each slice is one eighth. Two eighths make one quarter and four eighths make one half, so four small slices are the same amount as half the pizza.
facts.hook: an argument over who got more pizza

facts.fact: A year is 52 weeks plus one day, so your birthday lands one weekday later each year: a Monday birthday this year is on Tuesday next year. After a February 29th it jumps two days.
facts.hook: a child predicts what day the next birthday will be

facts.fact: Every number, no matter how big, is written with only the ten digits 0 to 9. Where a digit sits changes what it means: in 52 the 5 means fifty, but in 25 it means only five.
facts.hook: a price tag with the digits switched around

facts.fact: A long stick with a rock under it is a lever. Push down on the long end and the short end lifts a load far heavier than you could lift by hand, and the farther your hands are from the rock, the easier it is.
facts.hook: a stone too heavy to move in the garden

facts.fact: Dragging a heavy box across the floor is hard because the whole bottom rubs against the ground. Put it on a wagon or skateboard and it rolls easily, because only a tiny bit of each wheel touches the ground at a time.
facts.hook: moving a giant box of books with a skateboard

facts.fact: Pushing a heavy load up a long, gentle ramp is easier than lifting it straight up, though you have to travel farther. Movers use ramps to get pianos into trucks.
facts.hook: getting a wagon full of pumpkins up the porch steps

facts.fact: A pulley is a wheel with a rope over it. Pull down on one end and the other end goes up, which is how a flag is raised to the top of a pole by someone standing on the ground.
facts.hook: lifting a bucket up to a treehouse

facts.fact: A screw is really a tiny ramp wound around a post. Each turn moves it only a little way into the wood, which is why a screw holds tighter than a nail and takes longer to put in.
facts.hook: a wobbly shelf held by nails instead of screws

facts.fact: A zipper has two rows of tiny teeth that are slightly offset. The slider has a wedge inside that pushes the teeth together when you pull it one way and pries them apart when you pull it the other.
facts.hook: a stuck zipper on the morning of a snowy day

facts.fact: A refrigerator does not make cold. It pumps the heat out of the inside and dumps it out the back, which is why the back of a fridge feels warm.
facts.hook: a cat that loves to sleep behind the fridge

facts.fact: In a liquid thermometer, the liquid in the thin tube takes up more room when it warms up and climbs higher. The marks along the side turn that height into a temperature.
facts.hook: holding a thermometer under a lamp to fake a fever

facts.fact: A magnet sticks to iron and steel but not to copper, aluminum, or plastic, so a magnet can test what a coin or a can is made of. A compass needle is a small magnet that swings around to point north.
facts.hook: sorting cans and coins with a fridge magnet

facts.fact: Electricity only flows around a complete loop. A flashlight works because the battery, the wire and the bulb make a loop, and the switch turns it off by opening a gap in the loop.
facts.hook: a flashlight that will not work because one wire is loose

facts.fact: When you suck on a straw, you pull the air out of it, and the air pressing on the top of the drink pushes the drink up the straw. A straw with a hole in its side lets air in and will not work.
facts.hook: a straw with a tiny hole that will not drink milk

facts.fact: Each popcorn kernel has a drop of water inside a hard shell. When heated, the water turns to steam and pushes until the shell bursts and the soft inside puffs out, so kernels that have dried out never pop.
facts.hook: an old bag of popcorn where half the kernels stay hard

facts.fact: Hook-and-loop fastener has tiny hooks on one strip and tiny loops on the other. An engineer invented it after picking burrs off his dog and looking at their little hooks under a magnifying glass.
facts.hook: burrs on a dog give a child an invention idea

facts.fact: The gray stuff in a pencil is not lead; it is a soft mineral called graphite mixed with clay. It leaves marks because tiny flakes rub off onto the paper, and an eraser lifts them off because the flakes stick to rubber better than to paper.
facts.hook: a child afraid the pencil point is poisonous lead

facts.fact: Rub a balloon on your hair and it picks up a tiny electric charge. The charged balloon will stick to a wall by itself and make your hair stand up toward it.
facts.hook: balloons that stick to the ceiling at a party

facts.fact: Most maps put north at the top. If you face north, east is on your right, west is on your left and south is behind you.
facts.hook: following a treasure map that says to walk east

facts.fact: The Earth is a ball, so if you kept going in a straight line you would come back to where you started. The equator is an imaginary line around the middle where it is warm all year.
facts.hook: a child who plans to walk to the edge of the world

facts.fact: The land on Earth is divided into seven continents and the water into five oceans. The Pacific Ocean is the biggest; all the land on Earth put together would fit inside it.
facts.hook: a puzzle of the world with a missing ocean piece

facts.fact: Antarctica, at the bottom of the world, is a continent covered in ice with no towns; only scientists stay there. Penguins live there, while polar bears live only at the top of the world in the Arctic, so the two never meet.
facts.hook: a drawing of a polar bear chasing a penguin

facts.fact: The Earth turns, so the sun rises at different times in different places. When children in Japan sit down to breakfast, it is late at night in Britain and the children there are asleep.
facts.hook: a video call to a cousin who is in pajamas at lunchtime

facts.fact: The highest mountain in the world is Mount Everest, on the border between Nepal and China. Its top is nearly nine kilometers above the sea, where the air is so thin that climbers carry bottles of oxygen to breathe.
facts.hook: a child asks why anyone would carry air up a mountain

facts.fact: The Amazon River in South America carries more water than any other river on Earth. The rainforest around it has more kinds of animals and plants than anywhere else in the world.
facts.hook: a river so wide you cannot see the other side

facts.fact: The Sahara in northern Africa is the biggest hot desert, almost as large as the whole United States. Its sand dunes can be taller than a 30-story building, and days are very hot while nights can be cold.
facts.hook: packing a warm coat for a trip to the desert

facts.fact: On a flat map of the world, places near the top and bottom get stretched. Greenland looks about as big as Africa, but on a globe you can see that Africa is really about 14 times bigger.
facts.hook: a classroom argument settled by spinning the globe

facts.fact: An island is land with water all the way around it. Greenland is the biggest island in the world; Australia is even bigger, but it is so large that it counts as a continent instead.
facts.hook: deciding whether a rock in the pond counts as an island

facts.fact: A map's key explains its little pictures, and a scale bar tells you how far one centimeter on the map is in real life. On a map where one centimeter equals one kilometer, a town 5 centimeters away is 5 kilometers away.
facts.hook: a map where the beach looks close but is a long bike ride

facts.fact: There are about 195 countries in the world. Russia is the biggest and stretches across 11 time zones, while Vatican City is the smallest; you could walk across it in about 20 minutes.
facts.hook: a child who wants to visit every country in one summer

facts.fact: Some countries have more than one official language. In Canada, signs are in English and French, and Switzerland has four official languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh.
facts.hook: a cereal box with the same words written twice

facts.fact: Near the North Pole the sun does not set at all for weeks in the middle of summer, so children can play outside at midnight in daylight. In the middle of winter it does not rise for weeks.
facts.hook: bedtime in a place where the sun never goes down

facts.fact: About seven tenths of the Earth's surface is covered by ocean, and ocean water is too salty to drink. All the fresh water in lakes and rivers is only a tiny share of the water on Earth.
facts.hook: a thirsty sailor surrounded by water

facts.fact: Before electric lights, homes were lit by candles and oil lamps that gave only a dim glow. Most people went to bed soon after dark and got up with the sun.
facts.hook: a power cut shows what every evening used to be like

facts.fact: Before refrigerators, people cut big blocks of ice from frozen lakes in winter and stored them under sawdust in a shed called an icehouse. The ice lasted through summer and was delivered to homes to keep food cold in a box called an icebox.
facts.hook: an old tool in the barn turns out to be an ice saw

facts.fact: More than 4,500 years ago people in Egypt built the pyramids out of huge stone blocks as tombs for their kings. They wrote with small pictures called hieroglyphs on paper made from a river reed called papyrus.
facts.hook: a secret club writes notes in picture letters

facts.fact: Before cars and trains, the fastest way to travel on land was by horse. A horse-drawn coach could cover about 50 kilometers in a day, so a trip that takes an hour by car today took several days.
facts.hook: a child works out how long Grandma's drive would have taken by horse

facts.fact: A castle had thick stone walls, a water-filled ditch called a moat, and a drawbridge that could be pulled up. Its toilets were stone seats over a hole in the wall, so everything dropped straight down outside.
facts.hook: a castle tour where the guide points out the toilet

facts.fact: Before printing machines, every book was copied out by hand with a pen, and one book could take a year to finish. Books were so rare and costly that some libraries chained them to the shelves.
facts.hook: a child imagines copying a whole book by hand

facts.fact: Around the year 1450, Johannes Gutenberg in Germany built a printing press with movable metal letters. For the first time, hundreds of copies of a book could be made in weeks instead of years.
facts.hook: a class makes a newspaper with rubber letter stamps

facts.fact: Long before there were houses, people painted horses, bison and deer on cave walls using charcoal and colored earth. Paintings in caves in France and Spain are more than 15,000 years old and are still there.
facts.hook: a hand print painted on a cave wall by a child long ago

facts.fact: About 2,000 years ago the Romans built straight stone roads across their lands, with layers of stone and a curved top so rain ran off. Some of those roads are still used today.
facts.hook: a family walks a road that Roman soldiers marched on

facts.fact: Before coins, people traded things they had for things they wanted, like a sack of grain for a goat. Some peoples used shells as money, and the Aztecs of Mexico paid with cocoa beans, the beans chocolate is made from.
facts.hook: a playground trade of a sandwich for a toy car

facts.fact: Before washing machines, clothes were washed by hand in a tub, rubbed on a ridged board called a washboard, wrung out and hung up to dry. Washing day took a whole day of hard work.
facts.hook: a muddy soccer shirt washed the old-fashioned way at Grandma's

facts.fact: The first telephone was made in 1876. Early telephones had no dial or buttons; you picked up and asked a person called an operator to connect your call by plugging in wires.
facts.hook: an old phone in the attic with no buttons at all

facts.fact: About a thousand years ago, Vikings from Scandinavia sailed long, narrow wooden ships with one square sail and many oars. They reached North America almost 500 years before Columbus.
facts.hook: a model ship with one sail and a dragon on the front

facts.fact: The first tools were made of stone. People shaped knives and arrowheads by chipping flakes off a hard stone called flint, and they started fires by striking flint against a special stone to make sparks.
facts.hook: a sharp stone found in a field that looks like an arrowhead

facts.fact: Nearly 3,000 years ago, the Greeks held running races and wrestling matches at a place called Olympia every four years. The winners did not get medals but a crown made of olive leaves.
facts.hook: a backyard olympics with leaf crowns for the winners
